highlight.text: They brought over the Byzantine types of form and colour, the long lean limbs of the saints, the dark-visaged Madonnas, the blood-streaming crucifixes
highlight.lead: Anna Jameson on the models Cimabue grew up with:

work.text: The art historian Pietro Toesca attributed the Crucifixion in the church of San Domenico in Arezzo to Cimabue, dating around 1270, making it the earliest known attributed work that departs from the Byzantine style.

Its importance lies, in part, in the stylistic innovations and departure from some of the prevailing Byzantine conventions of the time, towards greater expressionism (especially in its portrayal of the agonies of death by crucifixion), empathy and humanism.

moment.text: It is closely modeled on the crucifix by Giunta Pisano, now in the Basilica of San Domenico, Bologna. … However, Cimabue goes further, especially in its portrayal of Christ's agony invoked by the contortions of his body.

matters.text: It displays the dying Christ on the cross, his eyes closed, his head resting on his shoulder, as his body buckles to the left. The sway of his rigid body indicates contortions brought about by pain.

Art historian Christopher Kleinhenz believes the move away from the Byzantine style was motivated by a desire to emphasise the "immediate, accessible, and human aspects of the deity", in line with the doctrines of piety emerging from both the Dominican and Franciscan orders.
